Subject: SLOs + warm-pool fast-path — recap and next steps

Hi Alyssa — thanks again for taking time today. Short recap from our call and a proposed lightweight test plan so we can validate the burst behavior against your SLOs. Please skim and flag anything missing.

High-level ask from RetailX (as we heard it today)
- P95 tail: <= 200ms for standard generate paths for 1–2k concurrent active sessions
- Peak bursts: up to 3k concurrent sessions for ~60–90s (Black Friday style spikes) with graceful queueing and no hard failures
- Streaming/first-token: initial token p95 <= 120ms for live chat flows
- Cost sensitivity: prefer short warm-pool baseline to reduce idle spend, but need fast fast-path when bursts arrive

Key technical notes (what Redwood will validate)
- Warm pools: recommended warm pool of N=16 warm workers (GPU-backed) positioned in the primary region; warm pool attachment should supply cold-start-free fast path for ~1k concurrent requests; plan to scale warm pool to 32 for the PoC to cover the 3k target with autoscale overlap
- Scale-up time: cold->serving node attach path ~45–90s depending on model size; warm pool handoff: sub-2s for requests routed to already-warmed KV cache on steady fast-path
- Queueing behavior: when concurrency exceeds warm+burst capacity, Redwood will enqueue requests with progressive backpressure and exponential retry hints; we will surface queue depth in the Console and expose a 429 vs 503 behavior matrix for you to consume
- Streaming semantics: continuous char/token streaming supported; we will instrument first-byte and end-to-end streaming p95 for the PoC

Proposed validation plan (2 phases)
1) Lab verification (72 hours) — internal Redwood load run to reproduce a 3k spike pattern against a representative model (same topology you run in prod). Deliverables: latency histograms, warm-pool hit-rate, scale-up timeline chart, queueing events log. (Attachment: redwood-slo-matrix.xlsx)
2) Customer PoC (1 week) — shadow footprint in RetailX staging with real-ish traffic from your replay tool. Deliverables: per-route dashboards, alert knobs, canary rollout and rollback exercises, final recommendations for warm-pool sizing and autoscale policy. (Attachment: warm_pool_diag_v2.pdf)

Immediate asks / next steps
- Alyssa: confirm the representative model size and approx 24-hour token distribution (avg response length). If you can share the replay artifact that’s the fastest path.
- Marcus: propose specific warm-pool sizes and a config that balances cost vs coverage for their profile (please reply inline).
- Lauren: I’ll need a short one-pager outlining risk & mitigation for our sales deck if RetailX wants an accelerated PoC.

I’ll queue a 30m follow-up next Tue; if you prefer sooner, tell me a window and we’ll shift.

Thanks — Evelyn

Eve / Lauren — quick technical note after reading Alyssa's model profile. A couple of points to make the PoC reliable: 

- Warm pool sizing: with 7B/4k we typically size a warm worker to handle ~60–80 concurrent lightweight streams (depends on sequence overlap). For a conservative start to hit 3k burst with headroom, N=40 warm workers is safer than 32. That assumes ~75 concurrency/worker -> 40*75 = 3k. If cost is a concern we can do staged warming: 20 workers always warm + 20 ephemeral to fill during day-of spikes.
- Fast-path routing: we'll pin a small subset of warm workers to the fast-path for streaming (keeps first-byte low). Those workers maintain hot KV caches and shorter prefetch windows. Expect <150ms p95 first-byte across most traces; the 100–120ms target is aggressive but achievable with tuned prefetch and region locality.
- Scale overlap tuning: set autoscale cooldowns so that when we detect a rising trend we pre-warm ephemerals proactively (threshold: 15% sustained increase over 30s). This reduces cold attach occurrences.
- Cross-region failover: warm-pool in US-East will have an added network latency; typical extra RTT ~40–70ms. Combined with our fast-path that's within the 200–250ms window for many requests but some tight streaming first-byte p95 cases may slip. Recommend routing only after warm-pool in primary is saturated, and use it as a last-resort fallback rather than primary failover.

I'll attach a short diagram (warm_pool_diag_v2.pdf) and a table of expected concurrency per worker (already in redwood-slo-matrix.xlsx).
